speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the immediate
question before the house is the subamendment to the amendment to the main motion on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I am rising at this time not to supplement anything that I have said or that anyone else has said but rather to try to make clear, as briefly as I can, our position on the immediate question before us, namely, the subamendment. In what I shall have to say I shall offer neither criticism nor commendation of the remarks of any hon.

member who has taken part in this debate. I wish to say that on the whole the debate has, in my opinion, been conducted on a high level. I think those who have spoken from every section of the house have given their best judgment to the consideration of the questions before us.
In moving his subamendment on Friday last, the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) asked four questions, I believe, and proposed certain principles or policies, seven or eight in number. He then moved his amendment which is expressed in four sections. Then the hon. member asked that we express our opinions with respect to the questions asked and that we state whether or not we concurred in the principles which he enunciated. I would not have risen at this time except that failure to say something might be interpreted as meaning that we were opposed to all of these things or that we supported them all, or some other incorrect interpretation might be put upon it. Briefly, I wish to deal wTith the questions now before us and I am glad to be able to say to the house that, as far as we are concerned at this time, this will be the last we shall have to say in the debate.
Speaking generally, I favour and we favour much the greater part of what the hon. member had to say. We approve the objectives he sought; and we agree with most of the means which he suggested for achieving those objectives. On the practicability and the utility of one or two of his suggestions I have some honest doubts. When I say that, I want the hon. members who represent the Social Credit party to feel that we are not in any way impugning their sincerity, or the faith they have in the principles they hold. If we do not agree with them in every proposal they advance we ask only that they give us credit for the same intellectual honesty that we give to them.
Let me refer first to the four questions raised by the hon member for Peace River. The hon. member asked whether the party I represent claims that under this government centralization has been intensified, taxes increased, the national debt increased to staggering proportions and bureaucracy carried to unusual levels. I do not need to make another speech to let the house know that the answer to each of these would have to be, yes. On several occasions I have said that taxes are five times as high as they were before the war and probably will remain four times as high. Our debt is four times as high or more, and our civil service twice or more times as numerous as it was before the war.

The Address-Mr. Bracken
With respect to the second point, the hon. member asked whether we claimed that the present government has in certain of its policies been introducing socialism while at the same time preaching a different doctrine. The nature of the debate I think answers that question. There is no doubt in our minds about it. Some of the legislation brought down, even at this session, leans toward totalitarianism.
The third question-and the house will pardon me if I deal with these briefly because I wish to get through by half-past five o'clock if I can-the hon. member asked is whether we believe that the government has been guilty of flagrant violation of its promises with respect to the men of the fighting forces. I shall only refer to one of the government's policies in order to answer that question. One has only to observe the housing situation to which these men returned to realize that the answer must be, yes. The inflated prices which young couples have to pay -for houses will keep many of them poor for half of their lives.
The fourth question of the hon. member was as follows. He asked if, in our opinion, the government had failed to preserve and vitalize true democracy in Canada, and if it had allowed conditions to develop which encourage the growth of communism and other forms of totalitarianism. One has only to recall two incidents in the recent history of the country to answer that question. One is the extent to which the cooperation of the communists was given to the government in the recent election and the infiltration of communists into the government service, resulting in the spy probe.
With these four criticisms of the general direction in which the government is going we are in entire agreement.
I come now'to certain policies or principles, upon which the hon. member sought an expression of opinion, upon which he sought either concurrence or non-concurrence. I do not feel that we have always to answer every question that every debater raises in the house; but, as I said before, in view of the fact that failure to do so might be interpreted either one way or the other and not leave the correct impression as to where we stand, I shall take a few minutes of the time of the house to make that clear. He asked if we concurred in these principles. Let me summarize them as briefly as I can and comment upon them as I proceed.
The first was that full and unfettered freedom shall be restored to the people of Canada. We agree with that, and I think by far the greater proportion of hon. members of nearly 83166-84i
every section of the house agrees. We agree with it to the fullest extent possible, short of infringement upon the rights of others.
The second principle was that all unnecessary controls, domination by state democracy, and centralization of power by a multitude of regulations shall be brought to an end. Mr. Speaker, the nature of the debate so far indicates where we stand on these matters. The answer is, yes. I have expressed similar views so often that there is no need of repetition here. I said so at an earlier stage of the debate.
The third principle upon which he asked for concurrence or non-concurrence was that crushing taxation shall be reduced by at least 30 per cent immediately. I have already said that on the basis of the government's own figures such a reduction should be expected. The hon. member went on to say that crushing taxation shall be reduced by at least sixty per cent within reasonable time. I am sure that W'e would all like to hope that that would be possible, but I am afraid I could not hold out such a hope and expect anyone to believe me, if the heavy commitments already made by the government and to which practically every hon. member is committed are to be carried out.
The fourth principle was that every Canadian shall be entitled to a social security income in addition to his earned income. This is being done now indirectly through the many social services provided by this country and, so far as I know, every hon. member has supported them.
Let me go on. He said that every Canadian should be entitled to a social security income in addition to his earned income, which would render him independent of state charity. I do not know that I understand the full implication of this statement. Certainly the purpose of our whole economy must be to enable everyone to have the opportunity of earning such an income, and the economy must provide it in cases where childhood, old age, accident, sickness or unemployment prevents it from being earned. But the hon. member's statement may contain implications beyond what I have suggested. Since that is probable, I shall refer to it again in just a moment.
The fifth statement of policy upon which he asked comment was this, that the paralysing restrictions on agriculture and industry shall be removed in order that the country's productive efforts may be free to enable adequate housing and other national requirements to proceed. I have been saying that for a long time. The fact is that all such controls as hinder production are a limitation on our
The Address-Mr. Bracken

standard of living and such controls should therefore be discontinued at the earliest time practicable.
The sixth principle upon which he asks us to comment is that farmers and other primary producers shall be assured a fair return for their services, and purchasing power sufficient to buy available goods. If I have said that once I have said it a thousand times in the last ten years. Jt is a basic part of our political creed. Practically every section of the house preaches that doctrine, though the extent to which it is practised by the government may be a matter upon which we would disagree.
The seventh point was that there should be brought about greater stabilization of wage scales and incomes. I know of no political party that does not agree with that objective. It must be obvious to all that this should be the purpose of any responsible government to the full extent that it is practicable in our complex economy. I am sure this government is endeavouring to reach that objective. But the test of government administration is in the results they secure. Certainly we must strive for these ends.
His eighth and last point was this, that parliament shall be made responsible to the will of the Canadian people. That is the principle upon which parliament was supposed to be established, and we must not depart from it. Then he added the statement that constitutional changes should be made to establish the legitimate rights of every Canadian.
If this means, to make the state the servant of the people and not their master, I am in entire agreement with it. I am in accord with the intent of my colleague, the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker), in seeking a bill of rights making this a basic feature of the constitution of the country.
I come now to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low). It consists of four clauses, three of which I can support and one of which I do not comprehend sufficiently to have confidence in it. The first part of the subamendment would return to parliament complete control of Canada's financial policy. I do not see how anybody could disagree with that. The second part I shall refer to in a moment.
The third part would remove present discouragements to the production and availability of building materials and encourage the construction of houses. Well, we have had a long debate on housing here and it will not avail us much to say anything more now on the question; but that is what we here have all been trying to say for many months past.

The fourth part of the subamendment would clarify the relative rights and responsibilities of the dominion and the provinces in our federal system of government. That is one of the things that I have sought for ten years or more to have achieved-the correction of the errors of the present relationship-errors which I believe every thinking person in Canada admits-correcting them with the minimum of centralization and the maximum of provincial autonomy. It was only upon the acceptance of these principles that this confederation was formed; it will be only with their maintenance that it will stand against the adversities of the future.
With respect to the second part of the hon. member's amendment, I have some doubt; and in expressing that doubt, as I said before, I ask that he give to us credit for the same degree of intellectual honesty in holding our views as we give to him in holding his. That part reads as follows:
The use of the national credit to meet at least some of the financial requirements for essential services-[DOT]
That is not the most important part of it; the most important part follows:
-and, as a guarantee that this country shall not again be subjected to financial depression, to make available to each and all Canadian citizens a proper portion of purchasing power which shall not first pass through the usual channels of industry, etc. . . .
And so on. Mr. Speaker, if society generally had sufficient faith that such a financial policy would prevent depressions-and if it will I am sure we all wish success to hon. members of the Social Credit party in propagating that doctrine-if that is so, I feel sure that parliamentary bodies would, before now, have given wide support to it. Since, so far as I know, they have not done so, it must be because society as a whole has not confidence in it. It may be the fault is in our society; it may be the fault of those who are promoting the doctrine; it may be that wre are too obtuse to understand it. At any rate, so far the doctrine has not been widely accepted.
It is a fact, nevertheless, that in some degree such a guarantee is given now; and to the extent that such a fiscal policy has been or may be used for the support of definite public services such as old age pensions, unemployment insurance, family allowances, floor prices and so on, services that are regarded as being essential to the public good, to that degree I support it and I am sure practically everyone in this house supports it.

The Address-Mr. Bracken
But, Mr. Speaker, if this part means, as I suspect it is intended to mean, the issuance of money or credit indiscriminately, apart from definite public services, and for no service rendered, then frankness requires that I say I am not convinced of its effectiveness or its practicability. I have tried to keep my mind open on this matter, but so far I have not been convinced of the soundness of such a policy. At the moment I cannot see it in any other light than that it would be giving, indiscriminately, to some people, the earnings of others. I can subscribe even to that for certain purposes, such as for the aged, for children, for the disabled, for the unemployed and for public measures of social and economic justice. But I cannot bring myself to support an indiscriminate policy-I emphasize an indiscriminate policy-which in my present view would have the effect, even though indirectly, of taking from those who work and giving to those who can work but might not choose to do so.
Let me summarize what I have tried to say. I agree wholly with the hon. member for Peace River in his indictment of centralization. extravagance, and high taxation. I agree with him when he says that the government is guilty of flagrant violation of the promises it made to the men of the fighting forces with respect particularly to housing. I agree with him in his indictment of bureaucracy, communism and totalitarianism in every form. Generally speaking, I agree with the objectives outlined by the hon. member and for the most part with the proposals by which he hopes such objectives will be realized. But with regard to the particular proposal, namely clause B of the subamendment relating to the use of the national credit, I have very grave doubts as to its practicability and its utility. I therefore find myself unable to vote for that portion of the subamendment since it might leave the false impression that I am in favour of this particular fiscal policy, when such is not the case.
